name: Hip flexor stretching (couch stretch)

image.caption: Hip flexor stretch – half lunge position

lead: The couch stretch holds the rear hip in extension with the knee bent against a couch or wall, lengthening the hip flexors and front thigh. It is widely recommended in posture and looksmaxxing communities as a fix for anterior pelvic tilt, with a flatter-looking stomach and better stance as the payoff.

It is thought to lengthen the iliopsoas and rectus femoris, which proponents say pull the pelvis forward when shortened by long sitting. Trials of hip flexor stretching have examined flexibility and athletic performance, including a 2021 meta-analysis; none found tests it for pelvic tilt or appearance.

paras: People hold the position for a minute or so per side, often daily, and pair it with glute and core work in anterior pelvic tilt routines. Changes in flexibility build over weeks.
No specific harms are documented. The position loads the knee and hip, and general guidance advises people with joint problems to seek clinical advice.

angle.text: The couch stretch is used in posture circles to lengthen the hip flexors and counter anterior pelvic tilt, for a flatter-looking stomach and better stance. Trials have studied hip flexor stretching for flexibility and performance, not pelvic tilt.

lead: Hip flexor stretching is a flexibility practice aimed at the muscles at the front of the hip, chiefly the iliopsoas and the rectus femoris of the quadriceps. The couch stretch is a popular variation in which the rear knee is placed on the floor with the shin braced up against a couch, wall or bench, so that the hip is held in extension while the front of the thigh is lengthened. [1]

In looksmaxxing and posture circles the stretch is discussed mainly as a way to reduce anterior pelvic tilt, a posture in which the front of the pelvis drops relative to the back. Proponents attribute this pattern partly to shortened hip flexors from prolonged sitting. [2][3]

Published research on hip flexor stretching has mostly looked at flexibility and athletic performance rather than pelvic posture or facial and body appearance. A 2021 systematic review with meta-analysis examined stretching of the hip flexors and performance parameters, and a small laboratory study examined hip extension range of motion and vertical jump. [4][5] No trial found in this search tests the couch stretch specifically as a treatment for anterior pelvic tilt.

paras: The iliopsoas, formed by the psoas major and iliacus, is described as the strongest hip flexor and as a postural muscle with a high share of slow-twitch fibers. It runs from the lumbar spine and pelvis to the femur. [1] In the couch stretch the rear hip is brought toward extension while the knee is bent, which also loads the rectus femoris, a quadriceps muscle that crosses both the hip and knee.

Practitioners usually hold the position for a period of time per side and sometimes add a trunk tilt or glute contraction. General guidance on pace and duration varies between coaches and is not standardised.

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and posture culture
paras: Anterior pelvic tilt is often described in online posture communities as making the stomach protrude and the lower back arch, and some say it affects perceived height. Hip flexor stretching is one of the standard counter-measures listed alongside glute strengthening and core work. [2] Encyclopedic sources describe this stretch-and-strengthen pairing as the usual corrective approach to lumbar hyperlordosis, while noting that the supporting references are limited. [2][3]

The Wikipedia entry on the iliopsoas notes that a short, tight iliopsoas is thought to contribute to pain in the low back, sacroiliac joint, hip and groin, but it does not cover stretching techniques. [1]

The authors of the 2021 meta-analysis open from the premise that tight hip flexors can contribute to lumbar spine pain and that sedentary behaviour limits hip extension flexibility; the review looked at performance outcomes rather than posture. [4]

No studies found on the couch stretch itself as a posture or appearance intervention. Related research on hip flexor stretching in general includes a 2021 systematic review with meta-analysis of stretching effects on performance parameters [4]; a laboratory study of 15 participants that compared pre-exercise static hip flexor stretching with hip extension range of motion and vertical jump height, whose title reports that changes in passive hip flexor compliance did not account for the jump improvement [5]; and a 2026 randomized controlled trial of high-volume, high-intensity stretching and its effects on muscle growth, strength and dynamic balance [6]. None of these measured pelvic tilt or appearance.

No adverse-event data specific to the couch stretch were found. Because the position loads the knee and the front of the hip, coaches often describe an intensity ramp-up, and people with knee or hip conditions are commonly told to consult a clinician; this is general exercise guidance rather than findings from a trial.
